title: 51/51 wins on a BTC mean-reversion bot, but I think the 100% win rate is hiding the real risk. Roast my setup.
author: bytecrawl
selftext:
I’ve been forward-testing a BTC engine for 30 days and want honest opinions before I trust it with anything real. *(Paper account, started at $10k.)*

**The numbers so far:**

* Balance: $10,000 → $22,472 (+$12,472)
* 51 closed trades, 51 wins, 0 losses, 0 liquidations
* Average win is \~$245, growing with compounding. Recent wins are \~$340 each after \~$85 in fees per trade
* 228 signals skipped because the engine only holds one position at a time. 224 of those would have hit target.

comments.author: FrostyFalcon-0
comments.body: 500$ in fees for 2000 in profit in only 6 trades? How?

replies.author: bytecrawl
replies.body: It’s because of leverage. Fees are charged on the full position size, not on the margin.

replies.author: Effective-Taro-4115
replies.body: What program is this? Can I use it in the UK ?

comments.author: koryuken
comments.body: If something is a very high win rate, I'm betting it's regime dependent. If you can cash in on the regime while it lasts, put a small amount of cash on it and ride it until it turns. I'm guessing when the tape changes the 100% win rate is going to look very different.

replies.author: bytecrawl
replies.body: Agreed, I think that’s exactly what’s happening. The bot actually trades both long and short (recently the signals have mostly been shorts), but either way it’s a small-target, no-stop setup. Choppy, range-bound BTC is perfect for it. A strong one-directional trend is what breaks it, whichever way it goes, because it keeps entering against the move.

replies.author: koryuken
replies.body: We both agree. Why not fix that in advance and add a long leg to your strategy. Figure out a hedge while you have time and be less worried about the tape breaking it.

replies.author: bytecrawl
replies.body: it already has a long leg. It takes both longs and shorts depending on the signal; the last 51 just happened to be shorts & longs both. I should have made that clearer in the post.

comments.author: cryptoman_101
comments.body:
The screenshot answers it: the target is 0.20% and liquidation is near 9.6% away with no stop, so you’re risking around 48 to make 1 and need near 98% wins just to break even. Your 98.6% hit rate is barely above that line. The margin implied by your open trade (−$2,849 = −12.7% of margin) is basically your whole $22.5k balance at near 10x, so one liquidation takes everything, not one trade. Trade #52 is already down around 8 average wins after 14 hours, and #049 sat −2.9% (near 30% of margin) for 17 hours to make $343. That’s 14 days of shorts in one tight range, not 30.   
  
The 51/0 record is what you’d see while collecting small premiums for selling a crash that hasn’t happened yet. Add a stop, and judge it by expectancy per trade, not win rate, before putting real money on it.

replies.author: Mytrill
replies.body: This is actually something I have been thinking about when I was doing automated trading (never profitable, just tried for fun). If all trades you do have a very close TP (e.g. 0.2%) and very far SL (5%, 10%). the signal's only job is to not enter at the absolute low / high, any future price action above 0.2% away from you guarantees a win, surely for highly volatile assets that should give some sort of edge? When I tested it it didn't, but I don't really know what I am doing. Anyone with more experience can explain me why this wouldn't work?

replies.author: bytecrawl
replies.body:
Good question, I didn’t understand this at first either.

If you set a tiny target and a huge stop, you’ll win almost every time, even if your entries are completely random. That’s simply because a small move happens much more often than a big one. The problem is the size. You win a little many times, then one loss wipes out all those wins. On top of that, you pay fees on every trade, so you end up slowly losing money. So a high win rate doesn’t prove anything here. What matters is whether you make money overall after fees and the occasional big loss.

replies.author: cryptoman_101
replies.body: You’re right that it doesn’t work, and there’s a clean reason. If price moves randomly, the chance of hitting +0.2% before −10% is just 10 / (10 + 0.2) ≈ 98%. That’s exactly the win rate where the small wins and the rare big loss cancel to zero expected value. Volatility doesn’t change it, because it brings both levels closer in time equally. The near-100% win rate is the payoff shape, not edge. Then fees break it: a 0.04–0.1% round trip eats 20–50% of a 0.2% target, which pushes the break-even win rate to near 98.4–99%. That’s above the near 98% the structure gives, so you lose about the fee on every trade, plus funding, plus slippage when the stop finally gets hit in a fast move. Not entering at the extreme isn’t enough. The signal has to actually predict direction, and that’s the hard part this setup only appears to skip.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: 51 for 51 on mean reversion usually means the losers just haven't closed yet. what's the deepest a trade went against you before it came back?

replies.author: bytecrawl
replies.body: The deepest so far was trade #022, a long. It went -5.07% against me and stayed open for more than 8 days before it came back for profit

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: -5% for 8 days is the real number in that post, way more than the 51/51. with no stop, the question is what the bot does when the same long goes -15% instead of coming back. is it sized so that one is survivable?

replies.author: bytecrawl
replies.body: Honestly, no. At10x leverage, liquidation is around -9.6%, so if a trade like #022 had kept going to -15%, the whole account would have been gone. It would have been liquidated well before -15%. Right now one bad trade isn’t survivable. That’s the biggest problem that I have been working on.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: then that's the fix before anything else: size it so a #022 that keeps going to -15% costs you a bad month, not the account. the 51/51 will look a lot less shiny at that size, but it's the version that's still around next year.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: You're right that the 100% win rate is the warning sign. A setup with a small target and a far stop wins often until one trade doesn't, and the open short in your screenshot is already deep in the red against its margin. I'd look at the worst open drawdown for each trade, not only the closed result, and check how a single big move against you would hit the account. Also be careful with the skipped signals, since "would have reached target" ignores the same drawdowns. Cymetica's Backtest Labs has a fee setting and a held out stretch of data for testing a rule like this.

replies.author: bytecrawl
replies.body: you can buy my api instead

replies.author: CyberJunky_NL
replies.body: Lol OP testet only 102 trades and is already thinking about earning money with it.. you haven't even started.. it's the losses who kill your bot.

replies.author: bytecrawl
replies.body:
Fair hit, and honestly that's the whole reason I posted. The title literally says I think the 100% is hiding the risk. 

Small correction: it's 52 closed trades, not 102. Even fewer, so your point stands even harder. The last short just closed +3%, but it was sitting around -12% of margin before it reverted. That's exactly the trade that worries me: a win on paper, but one bad trend away from a big loss.

What would you want to see before trusting it? I'm thinking a few hundred trades across a proper trending month, plus max drawdown and worst open position, not just closed P&L.

comments.author: pulllab
comments.body: I would judge this by the worst open trade, not the win count. A trade that sat 5% against you for 8 days tells me more than 51 small wins, because with 10x leverage that kind of move only needs to run a bit further to wipe out the run. Before using real money, I would set the size so that a repeat of that drawdown is a bad week, not an account-ending event, and I would also track expectancy after fees instead of wins alone. The paper run is still useful, but I would treat it as a risk test that has not met its bad case yet.
